title.en: Language work for Vitamin-M: prepositions, reported speech, question tags and sensory vocabulary

text.en: When Ravi spent time with his grandfather in Vitamin-M, every corner shop, banyan tree and question bridged two generations. Good grammar does the same: prepositions place events clearly, reported speech passes questions accurately, and intonation signals certainty.

Unit 4 highlights movement and sound words from the story: pottering, crouch, crawl, sprinting, darted and creeping name ways of moving; boomed, shrieks, whirr, thudded, grunted and snoring name sounds.
Prepositions link a noun or pronoun to other words to show direction, location, time or manner—such as 'walk across to the corner shop', 'fall over him', 'under the tree', and 'behind a big banyan'.
Look at the guided paragraph in Kaveri: walked through the village, crossed a bridge over a brook, found a quiet garden near a cottage, sat on a bench in the garden, strolled along a riverbank, and headed into the unknown.
Direct speech quotes exact words inside quotation marks; indirect or reported speech reports what someone said at another time or place without quotation marks.
Questions fall into two interrogative types: Yes/No questions starting with auxiliaries like Shall, Have or Are, and Wh- questions starting with Who, What, Where, When or Why.
When shifting direct speech to indirect speech: present changes to past, past changes to past perfect, present progressive becomes past progressive, and past progressive becomes past perfect progressive.
Pronouns and time-place words shift too: I becomes he or she, we becomes they, our becomes their, here becomes there, today becomes that day, now becomes then, and tomorrow becomes the following day.
Unit 4 also teaches question-tag intonation. Rising tone accompanies affirmative statements with negative tags like 'This is your notebook, isn't it?' when we feel fairly sure of the answer.
Falling tone accompanies negative statements with positive tags like 'You weren't in the library yesterday, were you?' when we are genuinely unsure and seeking confirmation.
Alternative questions with 'or'—like 'Shall we read this storybook or borrow another one?'—use a rise-fall intonation pattern: voice rises on the first option and falls on the final choice.
In the poem I Cannot Remember My Mother, sensory vocabulary is grouped into four senses: visual (glowing, gloomy, crimson), auditory (hiss, squeaky, ear-splitting), olfactory (aroma, pungent, fragrant) and tactile (sticky, rough, smooth).
Notice Sarojini Naidu's descriptive fill-in passage combines sensory words like scarlet, flaming, shrill and perfumes to bring a spring morning vividly to the reader's senses.
When preparing a personal caregiving presentation in Unit 4, organise clearly: background of the older person you helped, qualities you discovered in yourself, and what you learned about aging.
In magazine article writing on 'Our Inspiring Elderly', write the title and byline at the top, keep Paragraph 1 focused on the main idea, and pack Paragraph 2 with supportive real examples.

problem.en: Convert to reported speech and add the right tag: (a) Ravi asked Grandpa, 'What did you do today?' (b) 'You weren't at the park yesterday, ___?'

text.en: (a) Ravi asked Grandpa what he had done that day.

why.en: Past tense 'did' shifts to past perfect 'had done', pronoun 'you' becomes 'he', and 'today' changes to 'that day' with no question mark.
A negative main clause takes an affirmative question tag, spoken with falling tone when unsure.

prompt.en: State three direct-to-indirect speech shift rules (tense, pronoun, time word) and contrast rising vs falling question-tag intonation.

requiredIdeas.en: Present shifts to past; simple past shifts to past perfect
here -> there, today -> that day, now -> then, tomorrow -> the following day
Affirmative clause + negative tag uses rising tone (fairly sure); negative clause + positive tag uses falling tone (unsure)

commonMisconceptions.en: Keeping quotation marks or today/tomorrow unchanged in indirect speech
Using the same tone for every question tag

points.en: Prepositions (through, over, near, along, into) show spatial direction, location and time.
Indirect speech removes quotes and shifts tense backwards, pronouns and time/place words (here->there, today->that day).
Negative question tags after positive statements rise when fairly sure; positive tags after negative statements fall when unsure.
Sensory words enrich poetry across visual, auditory, olfactory (smell) and tactile (touch) domains.
